speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. To begin our assessment of your double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and upper limb weakness, please tell me: how long have you been experiencing these symptoms, and were they sudden or gradual in onset?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: The pattern of symptoms worsening with activity and improving with rest, along with diplopia on up/down gaze, strongly suggests a neuromuscular junction disorder. How long have these symptoms been present, and do you have any history of myasthenia gravis or thymoma?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: The absence of fever and family history, combined with symmetrical weakness and the classic fatigability you described, makes myasthenia gravis a leading suspect. To confirm this, I need to check for specific antibody markers and assess your ocular motility. REQUEST TEST: Anti-AChR Antibody; REQUEST TEST: Anti-MuSK Antibody; REQUEST IMAGES: Ophthalmology_Photos

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Anti-AChR Antibody: Present (elevated); Anti-MuSK Antibody: Not Detected; Ophthalmology_Photos: Ptosis of the right upper eyelid noted, worsening with sustained upward gaze; diplopia (double vision) observed with vertical gaze.
